name: LangGraph
question: How do I build long-running agents that pause, resume and survive crashes?
summary: LangGraph models an agent as a graph of nodes that read and write shared state. A checkpointer saves state after every step for each thread, so a run can pause for human approval with interrupt(), survive a crash, and resume hours later; you can also inspect and replay past steps. LangChain’s create_agent builds the common loop on top. It is the most explicit option for durable, controllable workflows, at the cost of more concepts to learn.
useCases: Workflows needing precise control of each step
Teams that want replay and time-travel debugging

steps.title: The standard loop, prebuilt
steps.text: create_agent builds the model-and-tools loop as a LangGraph graph. Custom graphs come later, if ever.

steps.title: A checkpointer and a thread per case
steps.text: Postgres stores the state after every step under thread_id case-8812. The in-memory saver is for tests only.

steps.title: interrupt() pauses the run
steps.text: Inside the tool, interrupt() stops the run and saves it. The request returns; nothing waits in memory.

steps.title: Resume from anywhere, any time
steps.text: A different process, two days later, resumes the same thread with Command(resume="approve").

steps.title: Side effects after the pause
steps.text: On resume the tool runs again from its start, so the dispute is created only after the decision and must be idempotent.

steps.title: Replay and inspect
steps.text: Every step is saved, so you can list the history, inspect state and replay from a past checkpoint when debugging.

practice.scenario: A fictional NBFC’s collections agent handles cases that run for days: it gathers payment history, proposes a restructuring or a notice, and must wait for a credit officer’s approval before anything is sent. Built on LangGraph with a Postgres checkpointer, each case is a thread. The agent pauses with interrupt() before sending, survives server restarts, and resumes when the officer approves, sometimes two days later.

industries.use: Collections and restructuring cases with approvals
Claims that wait for documents or assessors

practice.analogy: A case file that stays on the desk between visits: each step is written down, so whoever picks it up, even after a power cut, continues from the last page.

library.name: LangGraph + LangChain
library.what: create_agent builds the tool loop on LangGraph; a checkpointer persists every step per thread, and interrupt() pauses for a human.

practice.note: On resume the interrupted node runs again from its start, so keep side effects after the interrupt and make them idempotent (Panel 8).

numericDrill.question: A 10-step agent run takes 40 seconds per step and crashes at step 7. Without a checkpointer it restarts from step 1; with one it redoes only step 7. How many seconds of work does the checkpointer save?
numericDrill.answer: Without it, steps 1 to 7 run again: 280 seconds. With it, only step 7: 40 seconds. It saves 240 seconds, plus the model cost of six steps, and it avoids repeating side effects that already happened.

interview.question: How does LangGraph support human-in-the-loop?
interview.answer: A node calls interrupt() with the data a human needs. The run stops, its state is saved by the checkpointer under a thread id, and it can be resumed later, from any process, with Command(resume=...). Because state is persisted, the wait can be hours or days.

interview.question: What is the catch with resuming after an interrupt?
interview.answer: The interrupted node runs again from its start when resumed, so code before interrupt() executes twice. Put side effects after the interrupt and make them idempotent, and use a persistent checkpointer such as Postgres rather than the in-memory one in production.

mistakes.fix: Use Postgres or another persistent store
Place them after the approval, and make them idempotent
